channels.name: Identity, Auth & Access Control
channels.evidence: UP ONE, AND THE EVIDENCE IS MINE RATHER THAN A BUILDER'S — the rule is that no channel rises on a self-report, and this rises on measurements I took over real HTTP. Wave 9's verify critic found the lane's own work had not moved middleware at all ('unchanged this wave', md5 confirmed), so the escalation it reported was still live. I reproduced it: a READ-ONLY credential deleted a real issue FIVE ways — mc-role=owner 200, god 200, notarole 200, and THE COOKIE OMITTED ENTIRELY 200, a fail-open documented nowhere and reached only AFTER the session gate had admitted a human. The same forgery worked one route down on the db proxy, and that suite's own control test ENSHRINED it by asserting a forged viewer could still write a neighbouring table. And a successful login assigned an attacker-controlled `from` to window.location — verified live, evil.example.com/phish delivered into the page — at the moment an operator has just typed a password and most trusts the screen. All closed, all re-measured after: five variants 403, proxy 403, owner still 200. Sign-out existed as an endpoint with NO CALLER and now has one. WHAT KEEPS IT AT 6: `mc-auth` IS the password, so the session check is an unthrottled oracle — 30 wrong cookie values gave 30 immediate 401s while /api/auth throttles the same password to 10 per window, a ~220x differential in favour of the door with no lock. That needs the credential to stop being the password, which is a schema change, not a middleware edit.
channels.goal_text: builderz-labs — per-agent API keys and viewer/operator/admin roles over real sessions, replacing three shared passwords that double as their own tokens.
channels.next: mc-auth IS the password, so the session check is an unthrottled oracle — 30 wrong values, 30 immediate 401s, while /api/auth throttles to 10 per window. Needs the credential to stop being the password: a schema change.

channels.name: Portability & Host Independence
channels.evidence: npm install really was broken, on the owner's own primary goal, at step one. This host genuinely has no C++ toolchain, so a fresh copy failed the way a new user's would: gyp ERR! find VS. Not simulated. The builder traced the cause into npm's arborist source rather than guessing — the synthetic node-gyp rebuild step gates on pkg.gypfile !== false, and lockfileVersion 3 has no slot for gypfile, so resolving from the lockfile always reads undefined there whatever better-sqlite3's own manifest says. With the field added: install exit 0, npm ci exit 0, prebuilt binary used, no build directory. The better half is the durability gap it then found — a plain npm install silently strips that field back out on its next write — so there is a test, and I proved it myself by removing the field and watching it fail BY NAME, then restoring. A full clone-to-running trial was run TWICE from fresh copies: install, setup, doctor, dev, /api/health, login, an unauthenticated 401, then an authenticated create and read. HELD BACK: macOS and Linux are unverified, npm run build and npm start were not exercised (build is forbidden on this host), and a genuinely reachable Postgres was never tested — only the dead-endpoint path.

channels.name: Data Layer & Schema Management
channels.evidence: Migration 066 restores four columns that a live validator required and the schema did not have — environment, steps_to_reproduce, expected_behavior, actual_behavior — and DELIBERATELY does not add test_status, with both halves of that reasoning in the migration comment. The evidence for the split was measured, not argued: across 3,078 production rows in the Supabase export the stored test_status disagreed with the derived value on 372 of them, 12.1 percent, with passed sitting on rows whose tester and designer were both still pending. A stored duplicate of a derived value that was already wrong one time in eight. A new no-phantom-columns guard compares every column named in live code against the LIVE schema and is proven in both directions across writes, filters, selects and query strings — and states in its own header the case it would NOT catch, which is the interface declaration where this defect lived longest. WAVE 6 KEPT THIS AT 8 RATHER THAN RAISING IT, because a dialect asymmetry sat in the seam the whole time: an equality filter on a schema-declared BOOLEAN column bound a string, which Postgres infers correctly for free and SQLite never matches. Every Postgres-run test passed. The seam's two-dialect discipline is exactly what this channel scores, and it had a hole only the host a fresh clone actually runs could see. WAVE 7 closed the gap the previous fix could not reach and added a ninth guard for the class. Three columns are declared boolean in postgres and plain INTEGER in their sqlite twins, so the type-keyed hook was blind to them; no filter targets them today, so what existed was a trap whose trigger was 'somebody writes an ordinary filter'. The builder chose a curated override map over rebuilding two hot-path tables that every live agent-runtime wrapper writes to continuously, and deliberately did NOT leave a migration file on disk where an unattended db:migrate could pick it up before a maintenance window exists. I proved the new guard both ways myself, and — because this repo has twice shipped a guard that ran nowhere — confirmed the smoke test exits 1 with a gap planted and 0 without. Also measured this wave: the eq coercion works INSIDE an or(...) clause, which a critic had flagged as possibly a separate parse path.
channels.goal_text: builderz-labs — migrations run at first DB access, so starting the app creates the schema. No migrate command to know about, no colliding prefixes.
channels.next: Three boolean-meaning columns are declared INTEGER in sqlite; a curated override covers them, a table rebuild is the real fix and needs a maintenance window.

channels.name: Learning & Memory Loop
channels.evidence: The chain was already built — my briefing said 'nothing populates the store' and that was WRONG, the ninth wrong briefing this session; all four runtime adapters already called the exit hook and 37 tests were green. What was true is that the table held zero rows, so it had never been EXERCISED. A critic reproduced it end to end with its own vocabulary: real API transitions setting rejection_count by the app's own rule, a real spawn, a real row written on process exit, then retrieval on a task key that never existed, matching on FTS5 vocabulary alone. It also built a PGlite harness nobody had run and proved the Postgres keyword-overlap fallback is REAL, not a stub, with an explicit incomplete-scan flag so a bounded scan cannot masquerade as a complete search — it scored that as BEATING the competitor, which is SQLite-only. THE GAP IT FOUND: the exit hook never selected the issue title, so every lifecycle row carried a null title — and both engines index that field. A run finishing CLEANLY, with no rejection, wrote a row whose only searchable content was a task key the ranker deliberately strips: an unsearchable record. Fixed and pinned by a test that retrieves a clean run by title alone. A budget overflow now surfaces as 503 with its token numbers instead of an unstructured 500, with the claim reverted so an issue does not sit claimed with nothing running. HELD BACK: what was attempted, whether it succeeded, and the exit status are still null on every lifecycle row — deferred deliberately, since no real exit code is available at that call site — so a record says what was rejected, not what was tried. And the loop never closes automatically here because dispatch is off by owner directive.
channels.goal_text: Hermes Agent — records what it tried and failed after each task, retrieves it on similar ones by FTS5, and caps in-context memory so overflow errors instead of truncating.
channels.next: Filling `attempted` HALVES retrieval reach and nobody has measured it. The four production call sites had zero coverage.

channels.name: Customer Conversations
channels.evidence: The transport SEAM exists; the transport does not, and that is deliberate — the provider is an open decision on this board and no agent was allowed to pick one. What landed: a provider-agnostic inbound webhook with its OWN dedicated credential, idempotency (a real provider retries, and a repeat delivery now answers 200 duplicate with the original row instead of creating a second customer message), an outbound adapter interface with ZERO implementations that refuses an unapproved draft both at runtime and by type, and reply-level threading inside a conversation — migration 070, both dialects. The builder re-measured all four 'already good' claims instead of assuming them, including re-running the approve-gate CHECK constraint in both dialects and the draft-cannot-approve-its-own 201-then-403 against the live server. It also found a structural limit and refused to work around it: middleware gated every /api/* route on a session or the GENERAL internal secret before any handler ran, so its dedicated credential was correct and still unreachable without also knowing Todero's general secret. It wrote the diff and left the shared file alone. I applied it only after measuring all three refusals myself — no auth 401 from middleware, wrong secret 401 from the route saying 'refused, not passed through to any other check', and an UNCONFIGURED secret still refusing rather than becoming a bypass. Card verified in a browser: 'Who is waiting on a reply? / 0 awaiting approval' with the query printed. HELD BACK: no provider, so an outbox that cannot send is still a draft folder; and the VALID webhook path is proven at the route level only — the env var is unset here and restarting the server is forbidden.
channels.goal_text: Slack — a reply threads instead of drowning the channel. Grok Bot — drafts while you are away, surfaces only what needs approval. You approve; Todero sends.
channels.next: No provider. An outbox that cannot send is a draft folder, and choosing a transport is the owner's call.

channels.name: Live Agent Control
channels.goal_text: Paperclip — pause or terminate ANY agent at ANY time, and a hub-wide stop. The control is in the request path, outside the agent, so it cannot be reasoned past.
channels.evidence: MEASURED 2026-08-26 while answering the owner's question about Paperclip gaps. This is the third of the three capabilities BRIEF.md records for Paperclip, and it is the only one with no channel. The mechanism partly EXISTS and nothing judges it: GET /api/agent-pause?agent=builder answers 200 with a real is_paused/paused_at/paused_reason shape, /api/hub-pause answers 200 — and has ZERO callers anywhere in components/ or app/, so the hub-wide stop cannot be reached from the product at all. /api/circuit-breaker answers 200. There is NO terminate route of any kind: a running agent can be paused in principle and never killed. Starts at 3, not 0, because the routes are real and answer correctly; it is not higher because the one control an operator would reach for in an emergency is unreachable, and because Run Safety's automatic ceilings have never been observed firing either — so today there is no control over a running agent that has been watched working.
channels.next: Wire /api/hub-pause to a control an operator can actually reach, and decide whether terminate exists at all — a pause an agent ignores is a setting, and there is nothing to escalate to.

No terminate route of any kind

channels.name: Durability & Recovery
channels.goal_text: Any serious self-hosted tool — a backup you can restore from, taken without stopping the app, and an export that outlives the tool itself.
channels.evidence: ZERO COVERAGE, measured: no backup, restore or export route anywhere under app/api, no backup or restore script under scripts/, and nineteen channels that never looked. Todero is ONE FILE — db.sqlite, 1,288 KB today — holding every issue, conversation, order and run record. For something whose stated job is to run a business, losing that file is unrecoverable and nothing in the program notices. This is the only new channel starting at a true zero, and it is the one with the clearest claim to being a SHIP BLOCKER rather than a gap: every other channel makes the product better, this one is the difference between a bad day and starting again. Note the schema already survives a fresh clone — migrations run at first access — so what is missing is the DATA, not the structure.
channels.next: A backup that can be taken while the app is running, and a restore proven by actually restoring into an empty directory and reading the data back.

did: Found by asking what nineteen channels were not looking at
No backup, restore or export route or script exists at all

channels.name: Cost Attribution
channels.goal_text: Paperclip — a per-agent budget the run is charged against. LangSmith — drill from a cost number to the run and the step that caused it.
channels.evidence: The plumbing exists and has never carried anything. lib/runtimes/token-ledger.ts is real; the ledger holds ZERO rows and agent_runs holds ZERO rows, so GET /api/costs/breakdown answers 200 with an empty array — correctly, since there is nothing to report. Run Safety's goal names 'budgets per agent, and at the limit they stop', and a budget with no ledger to spend against is a number that can never be exceeded. Starts at 2 rather than 0 because the module and the endpoint are written and answer honestly. The case for this being its own channel rather than part of Observability: Observability is about whether a number on screen traces to a real query, and this is about whether the number EXISTS. The board's own spend figure was stale in three places until today for exactly that reason — nothing was accumulating it.
channels.next: Make one real run write one real ledger row, then make the breakdown attribute it to the run and step that caused it. Until a run happens there is nothing to attribute.

costs/breakdown answers 200 with [] — honest, and empty

channels.name: First-run & Hub Setup
channels.goal_text: Paperclip — create or join a hub and be working in it. The owner's words: "allow to create/join different hubs (similar to Paperclip)".
channels.evidence: Measured: components/OnboardingWizard.tsx exists, /api/businesses has SIX callers across the product, and one hub row exists — so a hub can be reached. But GET /api/onboarding answers 405, and the whole path from a fresh clone to a working hub with a project in it has never been walked by anyone. This is deliberately NOT Multi-tenancy, which is exempt: that channel is about ISOLATION — seeing only your own data — and this one is about a new person getting to a working hub at all. They can be answered separately and the exempt one does not block this. Starts at 3 because the wizard and the routes are real and partly wired.
channels.next: Walk it: a fresh clone to a named hub with a project and a first issue, without reading the source. Whatever stops you is the piece.

channels.name: Mobile Fidelity
channels.goal_text: Linear on a phone — every destination usable one-handed, nothing clipped, nothing that needs a mouse. The surface the owner actually reads this on.
channels.evidence: The layout foundations are real and defended: MobileNav carries lg:hidden, PrimaryNav carries hidden lg:flex, the two breakpoints must match, and scripts/smoke-test-layout.sh asserts all of it on every run after the responsive layout broke repeatedly. Sixteen tab components carry sm:/md: breakpoints. What has never happened is anyone USING it on a phone and reporting back — no channel has ever scored it, no critic has been asked to, and subagents have no browser at all. Starts at 4 on the strength of the guarded layout, and no higher because the layout not breaking is a different claim from the product being usable one-handed. The owner reads the flight board from his phone daily and gave eight pieces of feedback on it in one message; the app itself has had no equivalent pass.
channels.next: Drive the six destinations at 375px and report what is clipped, unreachable or needs a hover — starting with the surfaces added since the layout guard was written.
